result.summary: Pindar calls on young men to sing at the house of Telesarchos for his son Kleandros, an Isthmian and Nemean victor. He praises Aigina and its hero line, telling how Themis steered Zeus and Poseidon away from Thetis so she married Peleus and bore Achilles. The ode ends praising Kleandros and his kinsman Nikokles.

scenes.title: Song at Telesarchos' door
scenes.summary: Young men are called to sing for Kleandros; Pindar says the Persian danger, a Tantalos-stone over Hellas, has passed.
scenes.stakes: Hellas has just escaped the threat of Persian conquest; joy must not be lost to grief.

scenes.title: Aigina and Aiakos
scenes.summary: Pindar honors Aigina, daughter of Asopos, who bore Aiakos to Zeus; Aiakos' descendants were brave and wise.

scenes.title: Themis and the wedding of Thetis
scenes.summary: Zeus and Poseidon both desire Thetis, but Themis reveals her son would surpass his father, so she is given to Peleus.
scenes.stakes: The gods risk being overthrown by a son mightier than his father.

scenes.title: Achilles' deeds and dirge
scenes.summary: Achilles defeats Telephos, Memnon and Hektor, and the Muses sing at his pyre.
scenes.stakes: Achilles faces death in war, though his glory is secured by song.

scenes.title: Praise of Nikokles and Kleandros
scenes.summary: Pindar praises Nikokles the boxer and Kleandros the pankratiast for their victories.

The Muses, linked with Mount Helikon.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable reflection on time's guile and freedom as the cure for misfortune.
Compares the Persian threat to the Tantalos-stone hanging over Hellas.

analysis.text: The ode reflects relief after the Persian invasion; the Tantalos-stone image shows how near Greeks felt to disaster.
Heroic lineage and song confer immortality: Aigina's Aiakid heroes, Achilles included, live on through poetry, as does Kleandros.

legacy.text: The Tantalos-stone hanging overhead is an early version of the image later called the sword of Damocles.

fun_facts.text: The editor notes the ode may belong to the Nemean victory rather than the Isthmian, so its occasion is uncertain.

language_notes.text: "Portal" means the grand doorway; "recompense" means repayment, here the song as a worthy return for his athletic labours.
"Hath achieved reward of victory" means he has won a victor's prize; the archaic verb forms (hath, ye) mark the translation's elevated style.
The Tantalos-stone refers to the rock that hung over Tantalos in the myth, a constant threat. Here it stands for the Persian invasion of Hellas.
Pindar was born near Thebes. The "two daughters" are Thebe and Aigina, daughters of the river-god Asopos, both loved by Zeus.
The Oinopian isle is Aigina's older name, Oinone or Oinopia. The "queen of a city of charioteers" is Thebe, by the stream Dirke.
"Melley" is an old form of "melee", a confused close-quarters fight.
"Thereof" refers back to the earlier-mentioned story; the gods' council remembered it when Zeus and Poseidon quarrelled over Thetis.
The prophecy that Thetis's son would surpass his father echoes the succession myth in which Zeus himself overthrew Kronos; hence the gods' alarm.
"Heaven-sent prize" renders a gift from the gods; Peleus is rewarded for his righteousness.
"Ballot-leaves of strife" means the gods' contest over Thetis, imagined as voting leaves cast in a dispute; Themis tells them not to renew it.
"Mid-month moon" means the full moon; "unbind the girdle" is a traditional image for consummating marriage.
Telephos, king of Mysia, was wounded by Achilles when the Greeks mistakenly landed there on the way to Troy.
"Dorian parsley" is the wild celery (parsley) crown awarded at the Isthmian games, here called Dorian, i.e. Greek.
Games "of Alkathoos" are the Megarian games, named for a legendary Megarian king; Epidauros also held athletic contests.

context_notes.text: Aigina was an island near Athens famed for its athletes and for Pindar's many odes to its victors.
Aiakos, son of Zeus and Aigina, was ancestor of the Aiakidai, including Achilles and Ajax, heroes much honoured on Aigina.
Aiakos was said to have been so just that gods sought his arbitration.
Themis is the goddess of divine order and right, and she is known for prophetic counsel among the gods.
The children of Kronos are Zeus and Poseidon, brothers who rule sky and sea.
The sons of Atreus are Agamemnon and Menelaos, leaders of the Greek expedition to recover Helen.
The Helikonian maiden-choir means the Muses, whose haunt was Mount Helikon; in tradition they mourned Achilles at his funeral.
The pankration was a brutal combined boxing and wrestling event with few restrictions.

literary_notes.text: The Tantalos-stone makes the Persian threat a rock poised to fall, conveying lingering dread and sudden relief.
Time is given "guile", a crafty power that bends life's path, while Freedom is a companion who can heal.
Pindar abruptly addresses Aigina as "thee", making the praise of her union with Zeus personal and direct.
Compound descriptions like "ringing brazen melley" and "godlike sons" use Homeric-style epithets to elevate the Aiakidai as heroes.
The unborn son is compared to Ares in strength and to lightning in swiftness, foreshadowing Achilles' battle prowess.
The gods bowing their brows signals solemn, binding assent, showing the decision is final.
"Point the way to the house of Persephone" is a euphemism for killing, presenting death as a journey to the underworld.
Song is shown as a faithful attendant, with the Muses themselves mourning, to stress poetry's power to preserve fame.
Pindar compares the athlete to Achilles, lifting a contemporary victory to the level of myth.
